cells.tense: Right now you're watching something you kept alive pay you back.
cells.ask: Name one piece of it out loud to someone who watched you tend it — say what's growing and leave it there.
cells.core: You read the pattern underneath, and this time the pattern is showing you something that worked. Whatever you kept alive has come back as plenty. That way of looking isn't analysis for its own sake; it's the kind of notice that lets you enjoy what your own hands made. This is the good version — following the shape and letting the plenty sit with you for a minute without doing anything to it.\n\nThe thing to keep is that you can see it arrived. Not as a score, as a fact. The growth didn't happen behind your back and it didn't need your worry to stay alive. Tell one person who watched you tend it, or write it where you'll see it — one piece, named plainly. That's how this keeps feeding itself instead of sliding into need.
cells.sheetLine: What you kept alive is giving you back what you put in.
cells.verb: tending what you've kept alive and getting back the harvest
cells.place: the armature under the paint, where the shape keeps showing without the picture

cells.tense: You're braced for a harvest that hasn't come in yet, and you're guarding things nobody handed you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're guarding and give it to whoever's next in line, then go do something that has nothing to do with it.
cells.core: You're stocking a future nobody asked you to stock. Reading the pattern has gotten ahead of the growth — you predict what will need care, feel it early, brace for it, and care turns into guarding. None of that is bad in itself. The trouble is that the energy goes into a harvest that hasn't arrived, and the ease that was supposed to come with the fruit goes out ahead of it.\n\nThe good version is reading the pattern from the ground, not from the forecast. Let one thing go to someone else — hand it over and let it be theirs. That's not refusing to care; it's letting your care come down out of the future and land on something that's actually here, still alive and not yours to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending the next harvest before this one comes in.

cells.tense: You can still see the shape of things, and you don't trust that what it shows you will add up.
cells.ask: Follow something you used to love for twenty minutes without telling anyone it was practice.
cells.core: You can read the shape of things ahead of the room, and these days you don't trust that what it shows you will add up. Nothing gets said about why, and this isn't about the why. It's about what the quiet does — the reading goes underground, and the sense that what you look after ever accumulates goes with it. So you keep going without expecting anything to land, and then the harvest has nothing to land in.\n\nYou don't need a big project. You need one direction, chosen while nobody's watching, so that way of looking can come back through something you actually want. Twenty minutes on the thing that pulled you before you asked it to be useful. Follow it with your hands, not your worry. That's not a grand gesture. It's one place where the shape gets to be visible again.

cells.tense: You're already reading what's really there and the payoff is real, but you call it luck or other people's doing.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that did well and say out loud that you cultivated it, then name one piece you'll drop.
cells.core: The thing that made this grow is running in you — reading what's really there, quietly noticing how it works, looking after the parts others miss. It's working. But whenever it comes up, the credit goes sideways: to the season, the timing, the people around you, or the thing itself. The work's own momentum gets the name before you do.\n\nThat's what to look at, not the harvest. One item that turned out well, claimed out loud as tended by you. Then let one piece go — not as penance, as finishing. When you can say this grew because you looked after it, and then put something down, the plenty stops being a rumor you're standing next to and becomes something that happened through your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You grew this and you call it nobody's doing.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's care is already bearing fruit they can see; the record says growth has arrived, not that they have noticed it, so the bloom is described as happening rather than as something they can name. The reader could reasonably say the tending was never chosen by them, only inherited; no cell asserts anything about where the tending came from or what it cost. The ask survives being wrong because it moves the person toward the pattern they already work from, not toward a verdict about their harvest. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'what you've tended is bearing fruit' — it lets the card claim credit the person may not have given it — so every cell puts the claim in the person's hands or leaves it as a question.
